question: Rust Engine: What is pydantic-core, and what performance advantages does it provide in Pydantic V2?

options.text: pydantic-core is a high-performance validation and serialization engine written in Rust, compiling schema validation into native C-ABI calls for a 5x–20x speedup.
pydantic-core is an optional plugin written in pure Python that only activates when mypy is installed; without mypy, Pydantic V2 falls back to the same validation speed as V1.
pydantic-core is a caching layer that stores previously validated JSON payloads in Redis, so repeated requests with identical bodies skip validation entirely on the second call.
pydantic-core replaces Python's type hints with runtime reflection over docstrings; the speedup comes from skipping type hint parsing entirely rather than from being compiled to native code.

explanation: Specification answer: pydantic-core is a high-performance validation and serialization engine written in Rust, compiling schema validation into native C-ABI calls for a 5x–20x speedup.

question: Validation Modes: What is the difference between @fieldvalidator(mode="before") and @fieldvalidator(mode="after")?

options.text: - mode="before": Runs on raw input data before Pydantic performs any type coercion. - mode="after": Runs after Pydantic has validated and coerced the field into its target Python type.

mode="before" runs after type coercion has already converted the field to its target type, and mode="after" runs on the raw untouched input before Pydantic does anything -- the two names are reversed from their actual timing.
Both modes run at exactly the same point in the validation pipeline; the only difference is that mode="after" also re-runs automatically if a later field fails validation.
mode="before" only applies to fields with a default value, and mode="after" only applies to required fields with no default; you cannot mix both modes on the same model.

explanation: Specification answer: - mode="before": Runs on raw input data before Pydantic performs any type coercion. - mode="after": Runs after Pydantic has validated and coerced the field into its target Python type.

question: Cross-Field Validation: When should you use @modelvalidator instead of @fieldvalidator?

options.text: Use @modelvalidator when validation logic depends on multiple fields simultaneously (e.g. enddate > startdate or password == confirmpassword).
Use @model_validator any time a field has a default value, since @field_validator can only run on fields that are explicitly required with no default.
Use @model_validator only for fields typed as str; @field_validator is reserved exclusively for numeric fields like int and float.
@model_validator and @field_validator are interchangeable aliases in Pydantic V2; the choice is purely stylistic and has no effect on which fields are visible inside the validator function.

explanation: Specification answer: Use @modelvalidator when validation logic depends on multiple fields simultaneously (e.g. enddate > startdate or password == confirmpassword).

question: Polymorphic Schemas: How do Discriminated Unions allow parsing heterogeneous JSON objects with a shared tag?

options.text: It uses a single literal tag field (e.g. type: Literal["email", "sms"]) to match and deserialize into the exact target subclass in $O(1)$ time without trial-and-error parsing.
Pydantic tries each subclass in the union sequentially, catching the ValidationError from each failed attempt until one succeeds, similar to a series of except blocks.
It hashes the entire incoming JSON payload and looks up a matching subclass in a precomputed dictionary, so the tag field's actual value is never inspected at all.
Discriminated unions require every subclass to share an identical set of fields; the tag field only controls which default values are applied, not which class is instantiated.

explanation: Specification answer: It uses a single literal tag field (e.g. type: Literal["email", "sms"]) to match and deserialize into the exact target subclass in $O(1)$ time without trial-and-error parsing.

question:
During triage in Pydantic V2 Validation Routing, an engineer observes:
"Validation rules silently bypassed after instantiation: Setting p.age = -".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: By default in Pydantic V2, validation is only executed when the model is initialized (init). Attribute assignments on already-instantiated models (p.age = -50) are plain Python attribute sets that do not trigger validators unless explicitly
p.age = -50 does trigger the field's validator, but the validator itself has a bug where negative numbers pass an off-by-one boundary check; the issue is in the validator logic, not in when it runs.
Pydantic V2 disables all validation by default unless the model explicitly sets model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True); enabling strict mode alone will make this assignment raise an error.
The model was defined with frozen=True, which allows direct attribute assignment to bypass __setattr__ entirely, going around both validation and Pydantic's own immutability check.

explanation:
Root Cause: By default in Pydantic V2, validation is only executed when the model is initialized (init). Attribute assignments on already-instantiated models (p.age = -50) are plain Python attribute sets that do not trigger validators unless explicitly configured.

Fix Resolution:
Add ConfigDict(validateassignment=True):
